paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations describe a network through continuous dynamics. This paper investigates why their benchmark performance can fall behind models built from discrete layers. It identifies gradient estimation as one explanation: reverse integration in the adjoint method introduces numerical errors, while the naive alternative builds an unnecessarily deep computation graph. These problems affect how the model learns.

The proposed Adaptive Checkpoint Adjoint method records the forward trajectory and uses those checkpoints to establish the reverse trajectory. This addresses the accuracy problem associated with reconstructing the trajectory backward. It also removes redundant graph components and supports adaptive numerical solvers, bringing trajectory accuracy and computation-graph simplification into one training method.

In the reported image-classification experiments, ACA halves both error rate and training time relative to the adjoint and naive methods. The resulting NODE also exceeds ResNet in accuracy and test-retest reliability. Time-series results favor ACA over competing methods, and incorporating physical knowledge provides further accuracy benefits. These findings connect better gradient computation to stronger trained models in the evaluated tasks.
icml-2020-adaptive-checkpoint-adjoint-me.tldr: Adaptive trajectory checkpoints improve neural ODE gradient estimation, with substantial training and prediction gains in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to identify the best collection of K items in a cascading bandit problem. The collection is itself called an arm, and the objective is reliable identification under a fixed confidence requirement. The proposed algorithm, CascadeBAI, is accompanied by an analysis of how much time identification requires.

A central difficulty is that the amount of feedback available at each step must itself be estimated probabilistically. The authors introduce left-sided sub-Gaussian random variables, a class that relaxes the usual sub-Gaussian requirement. This makes it possible to apply a sufficiently tight Bernstein-type concentration inequality and derive an upper bound on the algorithm's time complexity.

The paper also derives a lower bound, establishing a benchmark for how quickly the problem can be solved. Comparing the bounds shows that CascadeBAI is optimal in some practical regimes, rather than across every possible setting. Extensive numerical simulations support both the algorithm's effectiveness and the tightness of its upper bound. The contribution therefore combines an identification algorithm with a probabilistic tool for analyzing uncertain feedback.
icml-2020-best-arm-identification-for-ca.tldr: CascadeBAI identifies the best item set with time-complexity guarantees that are optimal in some practical regimes.

paragraphs: A seller repeatedly posts prices to a single buyer whose choices account for future opportunities. The buyer maximizes expected cumulative discounted surplus, so purchasing decisions reflect more than the immediate offer. The paper assumes the buyer's valuation is a fixed function of a d-dimensional feature vector describing the good, and studies how the seller can learn revenue-improving prices in this setting.

The authors develop a deterministic algorithm based on bisection. Its construction combines techniques from integral geometry with an improved penalization mechanism that works with contextual information. These components address the buyer's strategic behavior while allowing the seller to learn from repeated interactions involving different feature vectors.

The algorithm has a strategic regret upper bound of O(log² T), where T is the interaction horizon. Crucially, this guarantee does not require a distributional assumption on contexts: it holds for any realized sequence of feature vectors. The result provides a pricing guarantee against arbitrary context sequences within the stated single-buyer model, including its fixed valuation function and discounted buyer objective.
icml-2020-bisection-based-pricing-for-re.tldr: A bisection-based pricing algorithm achieves O(log² T) strategic regret without distributional assumptions on the contexts.

paragraphs: Mobile health data can describe treatments whose amounts vary continuously, making dose selection a question of degree. This paper proposes structural nested models for estimating the causal effects of such treatments. The aim is to use those estimates to help identify treatment regimes that improve patients' short-term outcomes, linking effect estimation directly to a defined treatment-selection objective.

The authors introduce a quantity called the weighted lag K advantage. They define the optimal treatment regime as the one that maximizes this quantity. This gives the optimization target an explicit statistical meaning: a suggested regime is evaluated through the advantage measure the paper defines. The method also supports statistical inference for its estimated parameters.

The approach is described as imposing minimal assumptions on the data-generating process, rather than requiring no assumptions. Simulation studies and an application to the Ohio type 1 diabetes dataset suggest that it could provide meaningful insights for dose suggestions. The stated evidence supports its usefulness as a modeling and estimation approach for mobile health data, with the optimization specifically focused on short-term outcomes.
icml-2020-causal-effect-estimation-and-o.tldr: Structural nested models connect continuous-treatment causal estimates to a defined objective for short-term dose suggestions.

paragraphs: Universal probabilistic programming systems let users specify rich probabilistic models and attempt to automate inference for them. Their flexibility creates a challenge: a general inference engine must handle many unusual model structures. This paper focuses on models whose support, meaning the possible values or configurations involved, changes between program executions.

The authors show that existing inference engines can perform poorly on these models, often doing no better than importance sampling from the prior. This identifies a concrete gap between being able to express a model and being able to draw useful inferences from it. They introduce Divide, Conquer, and Combine as an inference framework designed to remain efficient when support varies.

The paper also shows how the framework can become an automated, generic inference engine within a probabilistic programming system. On three empirical examples, it produces substantial improvements over existing approaches. The stated contribution is therefore both an inference strategy for a difficult model class and a route to integrating that strategy into general-purpose probabilistic programming.
icml-2020-divide-conquer-and-combine-a-n.tldr: Divide, Conquer, and Combine improves inference for probabilistic programs whose support changes across executions.

paragraphs: Large annotated datasets can contain incorrect class labels. Many methods try to detect these errors using predictions from a model trained on the same noisy data. That strategy raises a basic question: why should a model exposed to incorrect labels still provide useful evidence about which labels are trustworthy? This paper supplies a theoretical explanation.

The authors prove that predictions from a noisy classifier can be a good indicator of whether a training label is clean. They use this result to design an algorithm that corrects labels according to the classifier's predictions. The corrected labels agree with the true Bayesian optimal classifier with high probability, giving the correction procedure a probabilistic theoretical foundation.

The correction algorithm is incorporated into deep neural network training. Models trained this way achieve superior test performance on multiple public datasets in the reported experiments. The contribution connects a practical heuristic to an analyzed correction rule: predictions learned from imperfect supervision can still guide improvements to that supervision. Its high-probability result does not assert that every corrected label is always correct.
icml-2020-error-bounded-correction-of-no.tldr: The paper theoretically motivates using noisy classifiers to correct labels and reports improved deep-network test performance.

paragraphs: Deployment often calls for networks that combine predictive accuracy with low memory use and latency. Deep but thin networks are one response to those requirements. This paper proposes a three-stage training procedure that uses a wider version of the network to help train the compact model intended for deployment.

First, the method widens the original network sufficiently and trains that larger network to convergence. Next, it initializes the thin network through layerwise imitation: the thin model learns to match the wide model's intermediate outputs from layer to layer. Finally, it fine-tunes the initialized thin network. The larger model therefore contributes learned intermediate behavior to the compact model's training.

A theoretical analysis using neural mean field methods establishes an advantage for the layerwise imitation approach over backpropagation. Large-scale experiments also support the procedure: ResNet50 trained this way can outperform conventionally trained ResNet101, while BERT base can match the performance of conventionally trained BERT large. These comparisons show that the training procedure can substantially improve what a smaller deployed model achieves in the evaluated settings.
icml-2020-go-wide-then-narrow-efficient-.tldr: Training a wide network first and transferring its intermediate behavior can improve the performance of a compact, thin network.

paragraphs: Variance-reduced stochastic gradient methods can solve large learning problems effectively, but their gradient-evaluation costs often grow linearly with dataset size. This paper proposes a hybrid stochastic-deterministic minibatch proximal gradient algorithm for strongly convex problems. Its aim is to reach useful optimization accuracy without always paying a cost proportional to the entire dataset.

For quadratic losses, the authors derive a complexity guarantee that includes a data-size-independent bound, with dependence on target accuracy and conditioning. They establish a nearly identical result for general strongly convex losses, with slightly larger logarithmic factors. These are guarantees for the specified convex setting, where the required accuracy and problem conditioning enter the analysis.

A central consequence concerns optimization error of order 1/√n, which the paper identifies as sufficient at the scale of the learning model's intrinsic excess error. At that accuracy, the stated gradient complexities scale as n^0.875 times logarithmic factors, enabling generalization-level accuracy with fewer evaluations than a full data pass in the analyzed regime. Numerical results also demonstrate computational advantages over prior methods.
icml-2020-hybrid-stochastic-deterministi.tldr: For strongly convex learning problems, a hybrid gradient method can reach generalization-level accuracy with less-than-single-pass gradient complexity.

paragraphs: Few-shot classification uses a small labeled support set to classify new query samples. LaplacianShot treats the queries jointly through transductive inference, using relationships among them as well as their proximity to known classes. It operates on a feature embedding learned from base classes and does not retrain that base model during inference.

The assignment objective has two parts. One favors assigning each query to its nearest class prototype; the other encourages nearby queries to receive consistent labels. Together, they form a graph-clustering view of the query set, guided by the labeled support examples. The authors relax the assignment problem and derive an efficient bound optimizer with independent, parallel query updates and a convergence guarantee.

Using ordinary cross-entropy training on base classes, the method is evaluated across five few-shot benchmarks. The reported results consistently exceed state-of-the-art methods across models, settings, and datasets. Inference times are close to those of inductive inference, supporting use on large-scale few-shot tasks. The findings highlight the value of organizing query predictions jointly without requiring complex meta-learning procedures.
icml-2020-laplacian-regularized-few-shot.tldr: LaplacianShot improves few-shot classification by jointly assigning query labels using class prototypes and neighborhood consistency.

paragraphs: This paper examines adversarial robustness through the representations that a classifier uses. It asks how changes to the input can affect the information preserved by those representations. The authors define representation vulnerability through the largest change in mutual information between input and output distributions under a worst-case input perturbation.

They then prove a theorem connecting that vulnerability to a lower bound on the minimum adversarial risk attainable by any downstream classifier using the representation. This makes representation quality relevant to what later classifiers can achieve. A lower bound identifies a limit on attainable risk; it does not by itself guarantee that a particular classifier reaches that limit.

Guided by this analysis, the authors propose unsupervised learning that maximizes mutual information under worst-case perturbations. The training objective seeks representations that preserve information even when inputs are adversarially changed. Experiments on downstream classification tasks support the robustness of representations learned with this principle. The paper thus links a theoretical characterization of vulnerability to a representation-learning objective and empirical downstream evidence.
icml-2020-learning-adversarially-robust-.tldr: Maximizing worst-case mutual information provides an unsupervised training principle for representations with empirically supported adversarial robustness.

paragraphs: Tree models organize a very large target collection as leaves, using learned node scores to guide retrieval. Their computational efficiency makes them attractive for recommendation and information retrieval. This paper identifies a mismatch between training these scores and using beam search at test time: training may ignore the retrieval errors introduced by the search procedure.

The mismatch can persist even when the individual node scorers are trained optimally. Good local scores therefore need not recover the most relevant targets through beam search. The authors develop concepts of Bayes optimality and calibration specifically under beam search, providing tools for analyzing retrieval quality in terms of the procedure actually used at test time.

They also propose an algorithm for learning optimal tree models under beam search, designed to eliminate the training-testing discrepancy. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the theoretical analysis and show improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The central implication is that tree-model training should account for how candidates are searched, because optimal node scoring alone can leave an intrinsic retrieval gap.
icml-2020-learning-optimal-tree-models-u.tldr: Training tree models for beam search addresses a retrieval gap that can remain even with optimally trained node scorers.

paragraphs: Few-shot learners must adapt from limited task-specific data. This paper introduces MetaVRF, a way to learn adaptive kernels within a meta-learning framework. It uses random Fourier features to represent kernels and treats the feature basis as a latent variable, allowing the representation to be inferred rather than held fixed across tasks.

The authors formulate training as variational inference and derive an evidence lower bound for the meta-learning setting. An LSTM-based inference network combines information from previous tasks with information about the current task. This context-dependent posterior inference provides a mechanism for sharing knowledge across related tasks while producing features suited to the task being solved.

The learned features can represent expressive kernels with a relatively low spectral sampling rate and enable fast adaptation to new tasks. Experiments cover both few-shot regression and classification. MetaVRF performs substantially better than existing meta-learning alternatives in some comparisons and competitively in others. The findings support adaptive kernel learning as a useful route to transferring knowledge while retaining task-specific flexibility.
icml-2020-learning-to-learn-kernels-with.tldr: MetaVRF learns task-adaptive kernels through variational random features and context shared across related few-shot tasks.

paragraphs: This paper develops a randomized optimization method for convex problems with linear constraints. Such problems appear in support vector machines and machine-learning portfolio applications. The proposed randomized primal-dual coordinate method extends a first-order primal-dual approach by operating on a randomly selected block of variables, offering a decomposition suited to large-scale problems.

At each step, the method selects a variable block uniformly, linearizes, and applies a Bregman-like core function to that block. These operations produce a simple parallel primal-dual decomposition. The algorithm's structure makes block selection and the core function central to constructing the updates, rather than requiring every variable to receive the same full update.

The authors establish almost-sure convergence and an expected O(1/t) convergence rate. A stronger expected linear rate holds under global strong metric subregularity, so that faster guarantee is conditional on an additional property of the problem. Implementation details and experiments on support vector machine and portfolio problems accompany the theory, with the numerical results used to verify linear convergence in the evaluated cases.
icml-2020-linear-convergence-of-randomiz.tldr: A randomized primal-dual block method has convergence guarantees, including expected linear convergence under global strong metric subregularity.

paragraphs: MoNet3D addresses the problem of locating multiple objects in three-dimensional space from a monocular image. Its outputs include each object's predicted 3D position and a 3D bounding box. The goal combines localization accuracy with processing speed, so the framework is evaluated for both the quality of its coordinate predictions and its image-processing rate.

The method incorporates prior knowledge about spatial geometric correlations between neighboring objects into neural network training. This makes relationships among objects part of the learning process. The approach uses those geometric relationships to improve 3D localization, connecting the prediction of an object's location to spatial information involving nearby objects in the image.

Experiments on KITTI report depth-prediction accuracy reaching 96.25% and horizontal-coordinate accuracy reaching 94.74%. The method also achieves 27.85 frames per second in the reported evaluation. These results support the paper's claim of accurate localization with real-time processing capability in that setting. The coordinate-specific accuracy figures describe the reported localization outcomes, while the frame rate addresses the separate question of processing throughput.
icml-2020-monet3d-towards-accurate-monoc.tldr: MoNet3D uses geometric relationships among neighboring objects to support accurate, real-time 3D localization from monocular images.

paragraphs: A contextual bandit learner repeatedly chooses actions using contextual information and observes noisy rewards. This paper considers rewards generated by an unknown bounded function with additive noise. It does not require additional structural assumptions on that reward function, motivating a method that can use the representational flexibility of deep neural networks.

The proposed NeuralUCB algorithm combines neural reward modeling with an upper confidence bound for exploration. It constructs that bound using a neural-network-based random feature mapping. The confidence bound provides a way to account for uncertainty when choosing actions, connecting a flexible representation to a principled exploration mechanism.

Under standard assumptions, the authors prove regret of roughly √T up to logarithmic factors, where T is the number of rounds. They describe this as a near-optimal guarantee and, to their knowledge, the first of its kind for a neural-network-based contextual bandit algorithm. Benchmark experiments also show competitive performance against representative baselines. The theoretical result remains conditional on its stated assumptions, even though the reward function itself is only required to be bounded.
icml-2020-neural-contextual-bandits-with.tldr: NeuralUCB combines neural representations with confidence-based exploration and achieves near-optimal regret under standard assumptions.

paragraphs: The score of a probability distribution is the gradient of its log density. Estimating it from samples is useful when a probabilistic model has a flexible density that is difficult to work with directly. This paper studies kernel-based score estimators, including approaches based on Stein's methods and score matching, whose relationships and theoretical properties had not been fully understood.

The authors place these estimators within regularized nonparametric regression. This shared framework makes it possible to analyze existing methods together and construct new estimators by changing the hypothesis space or the regularizer. Those choices determine the functions available to the estimator and how their fitting is controlled.

The paper provides a unified convergence analysis and proposes additional estimators based on iterative regularization. These methods obtain computational benefits from curl-free kernels and fast convergence. The contribution is both explanatory and constructive: it organizes seemingly separate score-estimation approaches under one framework, then uses that framework to develop methods with desirable computational and convergence properties.
icml-2020-nonparametric-score-estimators.tldr: A regularized regression framework unifies kernel score estimators and supports new methods with favorable convergence and computation.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks gather information from neighboring nodes, but those neighborhoods can mix useful signals with information irrelevant to the prediction task. Rich node features and many connections do not ensure that every edge helps. This paper proposes NeuralSparse, a supervised method that learns which potentially irrelevant edges to remove before they affect graph-based learning.

The sparsification process is parameterized by deep neural networks and uses both structural and non-structural information. Feedback from the downstream task trains those parameters, making edge removal responsive to the prediction objective. NeuralSparse can connect with existing graph neural networks, so the learned sparsification becomes part of how those models obtain useful neighborhood information.

Experiments on benchmark and private datasets show test-accuracy improvements of up to 7.2% for node classification when NeuralSparse is combined with existing graph neural networks. That figure is a reported maximum, rather than a gain promised for every dataset or model. The findings support the idea that selectively removing connections can improve generalization when neighborhood information includes task-irrelevant content.
icml-2020-robust-graph-representation-le.tldr: NeuralSparse learns task-guided edge removal to improve graph neural network generalization.

paragraphs: Robust Outlier Arm Identification asks which options have expected rewards that differ substantially from the majority. The learner adaptively samples their reward distributions to identify them. Unlike problems with a supplied numerical threshold or target rank, this setting derives its threshold from the collection of expected rewards, allowing the number of identified items to be unknown in advance.

The threshold uses the median and median absolute deviation. This makes it more robust to extreme outlier values than a threshold based on the mean and standard deviation. The formulation is intended for applications such as identifying promising drugs or population-favored items, where the goal is to discover a set rather than choose a predetermined number.

The authors propose two algorithms with δ-PAC guarantees, including a UCB-style outlier-detection algorithm, and derive sample-complexity upper bounds. A worst-case lower bound matches up to logarithmic factors, supporting the general tightness of those guarantees. Experiments report robustness and roughly fivefold better sample efficiency than state-of-the-art methods in the evaluated comparisons.
icml-2020-robust-outlier-arm-identificat.tldr: Robust, data-dependent thresholds enable adaptive outlier identification with near-matching sample-complexity bounds.

paragraphs: When several algorithms analyze sensitive data in sequence, their privacy guarantees must be combined. The resulting composition bound describes how the overall guarantee degrades as analyses accumulate. This paper develops sharper analytical bounds for that accounting problem within the framework of f-differential privacy, with Gaussian differential privacy providing the setting highlighted by the title.

The method uses an Edgeworth expansion to refine the approximation underlying composition analysis. Existing composition results can rely on the central limit theorem; the proposed approach uses a more accurate approximation to obtain tighter bounds. Its contribution concerns how precisely accumulated privacy is quantified, making the mathematical approximation central to the resulting guarantee.

The authors describe the method as easy to implement and computationally efficient for any number of compositions. They support its improved tightness through asymptotic error analysis and an application to noisy stochastic gradient descent for private deep-network training. Together, these results connect a refined analytical technique to a practical privacy-accounting problem involving many sequential algorithmic steps.
icml-2020-sharp-composition-bounds-for-g.tldr: Edgeworth expansions provide tighter, computationally efficient privacy composition bounds than central-limit-based approximations.

paragraphs: Regression forests combine multiple trees to predict numerical outcomes. Their effectiveness often depends on trees built by greedy, top-down procedures such as CART. This paper asks how much the forest can improve when the method for optimizing each tree changes, focusing on tree learning as a source of better ensemble performance.

The authors extend Tree Alternating Optimization, previously developed for classification trees, to regression. They combine it with bagging to build forests of oblique trees. These trees use hyperplane decisions at their internal nodes, giving each split a form that can involve combinations of input features. The approach therefore brings an alternative tree optimizer into the construction of regression ensembles.

Across a wide range of datasets, the resulting forests outperform random forests, AdaBoost, and gradient boosting in accuracy, often considerably. They also usually contain fewer and shallower trees, producing fewer parameters and faster overall inference. These are empirical findings with explicit qualifications: the size advantages are usual, not universal. The results show that improved tree optimization can benefit both prediction quality and deployment efficiency.
icml-2020-smaller-more-accurate-regressi.tldr: Tree Alternating Optimization produces regression forests that are more accurate and usually smaller and faster in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Standard multi-armed bandit formulations emphasize reward while balancing exploration and exploitation. In applications where variability matters, the average reward alone may not capture the decision maker's objective. This paper studies mean-variance bandits, which incorporate risk through an objective that accounts for both expected reward and reward variation.

The authors develop Thompson Sampling-style algorithms for this setting and analyze their regret for Gaussian and Bernoulli reward distributions. Their motivation includes reducing the unrealistic distributional assumptions used by existing mean-variance methods. The analysis therefore addresses both how the algorithms learn and what assumptions support their performance guarantees within these two distribution families.

The algorithms achieve the best known regret bounds reported for mean-variance bandits and reach information-theoretic bounds in some parameter regimes. This optimality claim is restricted to those regimes. Empirical simulations show substantial improvements over existing lower-confidence-bound algorithms across all risk tolerances evaluated. The work extends sampling-based exploration to risk-sensitive objectives while supporting it with both regret analysis and numerical comparisons.
icml-2020-thompson-sampling-algorithms-f.tldr: Thompson Sampling-style methods improve mean-variance bandit regret guarantees and outperform LCB methods in the reported simulations.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses unlabeled examples alongside limited labeled data. A common approach asks the model to produce consistent outputs for similar examples or augmentations. This paper points out that predictions on an unlabeled example can change substantially across training stages, creating noisy or conflicting objectives that may contribute to concept drift and catastrophic forgetting.

The proposed approach gives priority to unlabeled examples whose outputs remain more consistent over time. Under this selection rule, training combines two self-supervised losses. A consistency loss aligns an example with its augmentation, while a contrastive loss encourages different examples to have different outputs. Temporal stability thus guides which unlabeled examples are used first.

The authors show that this time-consistent selection can improve final test accuracy while reducing computation. Their complete method achieves state-of-the-art results on several semi-supervised benchmarks with substantially less computation. The findings make training dynamics part of the data-selection strategy: the usefulness of an unlabeled example depends partly on how reliably the model treats it over the course of learning.
icml-2020-time-consistent-self-supervisi.tldr: Prioritizing unlabeled examples with stable predictions over time improves semi-supervised accuracy and reduces computation in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Particle-based variational inference approximates a target distribution by optimizing a collection of particles. Methods such as Stein Variational Gradient Descent have been proposed as efficient approximate inference procedures and possible alternatives to MCMC. This paper examines the quality of the posterior approximations they produce in large-scale Bayesian inference, making particle sample quality central to the evaluation.

The analysis finds that existing particle methods using stochastic gradients converge too slowly under sample-quality metrics. To address this, the authors propose a framework combining variance reduction with quasi-Newton preconditioning. They build the framework using the Riemannian structure of Wasserstein space and advanced Riemannian optimization methods, connecting the optimization changes to the geometry of distributions.

Experiments demonstrate accelerated convergence for accurate posterior inference in large-scale and ill-conditioned problems. The contribution concerns how quickly the particles form a useful approximation, rather than merely whether optimization can be performed. It also highlights the importance of evaluating the resulting posterior samples when judging the practical efficiency of particle-based inference methods.
icml-2020-variance-reduction-and-quasi-n.tldr: Variance reduction and quasi-Newton preconditioning accelerate particle-based posterior inference in large-scale and ill-conditioned problems.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning usually treats the reward function as a fixed description of what an agent should achieve. This paper investigates whether the reward function can itself store learned knowledge. The authors propose a scalable meta-gradient framework that learns useful intrinsic rewards across multiple lifetimes of experience, making the reward signal an object of learning.

Their proof-of-concept experiments examine whether those rewards can encode knowledge about long-term exploration and exploitation. The reported results show that this is feasible. A learned reward can guide what an agent pursues, allowing experience accumulated across lifetimes to influence later learning through the objective supplied to the agent.

The paper also reports generalization to other kinds of agents and to changes in environmental dynamics. It distinguishes this transfer from transferring a policy: a reward describes desirable outcomes, while a policy captures behavior. The experiments support the possibility that knowledge about objectives can remain useful when the agent or its environment changes. The evidence is presented as proof of concept, rather than a universal transfer guarantee.
icml-2020-what-can-learned-intrinsic-rew.tldr: Learned intrinsic rewards can capture exploration and exploitation knowledge that transfers across agents and environmental changes in proof-of-concept experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies pricing a single product when demand grows over time in expectation and may also become more variable. The seller sequentially chooses prices while learning an unknown demand model, seeking to maximize expected cumulative revenue. The non-stationary setting makes both the growth of demand and the evolution of its random fluctuations relevant to learning.

The authors prove matching upper and lower regret bounds and provide near-optimal pricing policies. Their analysis shows how the rate of growth in demand fluctuations affects achievable regret and policy design. It also finds that knowing the time horizon in advance can change the optimal regret order, making advance knowledge of the selling period theoretically consequential.

An extension permits the optimal price itself to vary with time and supplies a near-optimal policy for that model. The paper also analyzes an analogous growing, non-stationary multi-armed bandit setting. There, knowing the horizon does not change the optimal regret order. This contrast identifies a meaningful difference between the pricing problem and its bandit analogue.
icml-2020-when-demands-evolve-larger-and.tldr: For growing, increasingly noisy demand, optimal pricing regret depends on fluctuation growth and whether the seller knows the time horizon.
